what i take from the study isn't that there's any particular switch once you go over 90 minutes, but as you increase exercise duration, the risks can go up.

take triathletes for example. we have three sports to train for and generally want to become pretty proficient at them. we tend to be a-type personalities, often in high pressure jobs with limited time to train for endurance events (i don't personally fit those first two). the sports can totally be an escape for us, but we can also put intense pressure on ourselves to train more to get faster and eke out those marginal gains. seriously, plenty of us will not bat an eye at dropping thousands of dollars to save a couple minutes over a 10 hour race (again, not me).

i think other athletic endeavors can run into similar issues too. consider body builders spending hours every week for tiny gains, cutting constantly to make various muscles pop.

competitive swimmers spending hours every day, twice a day to shave fractions of a second off their pb, and then when the race season ends...depression (see: phelps).

i imagine a lot of fitness people, especially now with ig face similar pressure. they have to constantly post and constantly work out and put their body out there. you can't fake it like a fashion blogger who can wear an outfit for 5 minutes, take a bunch of photos and in a few hours in one day make it look like you're doing all this shit. because you can't say you're doing all this lifting if your body doesn't show it. plus the whole body dysmorphia aspect and the pressure to shill posts for sponsors every day.

i think it really boils down to how you treat the exercise. you can casually cycle for 90 minutes every day and use it as basically free therapy. you can do the same thing with swimming. if you aren't putting pressure on yourself then you're unlikely to face any repercussions, but the more personal pressure you face the more the risks go up, especially if you find yourself not hitting your targets.

3. regarding laying down, i don't resist this urge. lying prone, ideally with a book in hand, is my favorite position in life. it's like the only time i don't feel pain, both physical and existential. but, instead of resisting this urge, i make time for this urge and direct it into healthy nothingness. the structure/designated time also helps me get the most out of it because i can look forward to it, instead of feeling sucked into it. i get in my bed at 9 to just lay for an hour and calm down, read, reddit, etc so that sleep comes so easily between 10 and 10:30. if i can't guarantee that time, i set aside time elsewhere. sometimes i just lay on my yoga mat at the gym after a good workout. 

sweet sweet nothing time. i cherish it. it's the only way i feel fully human. which is how i want to address the fact that fitness challenges people in different degrees in different ways, even on different days! i struggle with a mood disorder and a sensory disorder due to ptsd. sometimes focusing all my available fucks on finishing a work day leaves me empty. those days, i'm not trying to overextend my available energy by pring at the gym. i "get back on the horse," as the books say, but i don't have to go full gallop. sometimes, even when i'm following a gym routine, i say "fuck it," and do what i think would feel good or, miraculously, restore energy. afterwards, i'm gonna go home and do the necessities, like make a healthy-but-lowkey dinner and maybe pay a bill, or two if i'm feeling dangerous. not every day needs to be exploited and not every day needs to be a challenge. and, \*gasp\* *sometimes i don't go to the gym*. if i have to choose, on a low energy day, between the gym and having enough energy to clean the house, preparing for work the next day, plan the weekend, read some more of that book, and not feel like i wanna kill myself, then i am not choosing the gym.

2. trying, failing and trying again. find out what works best for you. schedules, to-do lists, time-management tools, habit apps, whatever. personally, i'm super motivated by long-term calendars (so i don't feel like time is slipping away) and keeping a weekly/daily diary to look back on and go "fuck yeah!" huuuge sense of accomplishment there. i'm also motivated by goals and projects. if i need to renovate in my house, i'll set a party a couple months out so i have a deadline. i'm gonna do a tri in a month because two weeks ago i realized that i wasn't progressing my cardio because i had nothing to prepare for. past goals have been a half marathon, a bike tour or even a day of rock climbing at a pricey gym to motivate my lifting. speaking of language learning, i have 6 months to become conversational in german so i can go with my partner to her hometown in switzerland and meet her dad who doesn't speak english well. talk about a motivating timeline! finally, to make these goals achievable, i live by a structured schedule on weekdays with flexibility structured into the weekend.

i’m 5’6” and around 160 right now. just over the top of a healthy bmi. i don’t think i’ll ever overcome body image issues entirely, but i’m in a healthier place mentally than i’ve ever been from almost a year of reframing the way i look at diet, exercise, and myself through:

1. non-scale and aesthetic goals - smart goals don’t really work well for me. i wanted to climb mountains. so i started climbing mountains. and then tougher mountains. i thought i was too socially anxious group exercise.    so i tried bikram yoga, sucked at it, kept with it, and now i suck less at it. i decided to go on my first run since middle school. so i did. and then signed up for a half marathon. and ran it. in the next 6 months, i’m going to finish my peakbagging list, run a marathon, and fingers crossed, feel comfortable enough in my body (no matter what it looks like), to bare my midriff at bikram and the beach.

2. what i consider failure - i remind myself that having days where i overeat or days where i skip exercise are not punishable offenses and that emotional/physical self-harm is just exacerbating the issue. i analyze and reevaluate the standards i set for myself much more often and don’t let myself be as harsh. even when i think my goals are reasonable and i press snooze 1,000x or stay in to read on the couch instead of running in the rain, i look at as something i needed and get back in it the next day or week or even month. it’s really hard and i still have binge/purge slip ups but they’re coming less and less frequently. 

3. the way i talk about my body - i would never think or talk as nastily about my friends’ and family’s bodies as i do about my own. plus, when i do, it hurts people who don’t know it’s about my own self-hatred and not particular features they may have as well. overtime, focusing on them less has helped me like my “problem areas” a lot more.

4. how other people talk about my body or fatness/fitness in general - i’m a lot more assertive about telling people their words are unkind or inappropriate and that their opinions on body type or fitness level are simplistic or prejudiced. sometimes it feels a little bit spiteful, but it’s satisfying and i think good if it even occasionally has the effect of people being kinder to themselves and others.

not sure why you doubt that. i run/walk or just walk 90 minutes to 2.5 hours regularly. if you live in a walkable area, it's very easy to end up doing this. if you are, as op states, looking for mental health benefits then this extended time can be very helpful in changing your outlook on life. she drinks coffee midway and seems to incorporate this activity into an extended morning routine. i totally get wanting to have the higher mileage/more time out there even if your running fitness/base isn't there yet. my personal route to improvement with this has been using intervals. break the run into consistent run/walk intervals & gradually increase the run & reduce the walks. pace will increase pretty naturally.

as for weight loss, i think we just don't know enough about op to make more than general suggestions. she describes herself as overweight, but we don't know what that means. many women describe themselves as overweight but are actually healthy. personally, i found that weight loss became much harder after 40 and calorie restriction becomes a much more challenging way to achieve it. for women over 40, keeping your basic metabolism up is critical. this means maintaining or even building lean muscle mass - either through bursts of intense intervals and/or weightlifting. otherwise, you just find you have to eat less & less via calorie restriction. my own experience is that running did help me lose weight pretty easily as my mileage & pace increased. op might start by just focusing on conscious eating: what food feels like it sustains a more active lifestyle; stopping eating before "full" (which is often over-full); paying more attention to and enjoying food rather than mindlessly eating; cutting back on unhealthy snacks & mindless eating. look for easy cuts (soda, candy) that are high-calorie, low-nutrition/energy. but again, i think adding some bursts of intensity in running (short ones) will help pace, calorie burn & can encourage healthier eating choices to sustain it.
